1:
Who the man addressed is they cannot agree. Gill lays out three readings without choosing: the Gentiles, particularly the seemingly virtuous who reproved others and did the same, as Socrates, Cato and Seneca; the Jews, who despised the Gentiles while thinking themselves right; or magistrates of either nation, who punish sin and so must know the law. Calvin takes it of neither nation but of a kind: hypocrites who dazzle men's eyes by displays of outward sanctity, saintlings not included in the first catalogue of grosser vices. Henry allows the general terms may reach those many masters of whatever nation who assume a power to censure and condemn, but holds the Jews especially intended. Barnes makes the generality deliberate: naming the Jews openly would have excited their opposition, so Paul affirms it of man and applies it only later, when his premises are too far advanced to evade. Wesley reads the bare appellation the same way: Paul calls him only O man, as not acknowledging him to be a Jew. Robertson keeps it wider, a statement applicable to all, since the Gentile is readily condemned by the Jew and equally the Jew by the Gentile; Ellicott says the description of one section of the race implicitly condemns the other. Clarke does not argue the point, his block being an analysis of the whole chapter.

What the opening Therefore refers back to is sharper. Barnes says the force of the word has been much discussed and refers it to no particular word or verse but to the general considerations of the whole case. Calvin admits that most confess the illative can hardly be accounted for, the inference from what precedes being unclear; his own view is that it is a Hebraism looking forward rather than back, anticipating a reason given afterwards, so that the sense is: on this account inexcusable art thou, because in condemning another thou condemnest thyself. Robertson refers it back to the earlier chapter, because of which thing. Wesley makes it the hinge, the transition from Gentiles to Jews until the sixth verse comprises both.

The two Greek verbs divide them again. Robertson insists the first does not of itself mean to condemn but to pick out, separate, approve. Barnes allows it is the weaker of the two but takes it here of condemning, implying that the Jews expressed themselves freely and severely on the character and doom of the Gentiles, whom they regarded with abhorrence. Ellicott makes the pair procedural: they stand as a judge's summing up to his verdict, in the first sentence still being passed with a possibility of acquittal, in the second definitely given against the accused; another, he adds, is strictly thy fellow or neighbour. Calvin notes the striking resemblance of the two words and reads the first as condemning.

Why the guilt is aggravated they answer alike. Henry argues from the light: if the Gentiles, who had but the light of nature, were inexcusable, much more the Jews, who had the law and the revealed will of God. Barnes says the same, and adds that inexcusable does not mean inexcusable for judging but under condemnation for their own crimes and needing another plan of justification. Wesley puts it in a line: knowledge without practice only increases guilt. Calvin calls them doubly deserving of condemnation, and observes that in reproving a thief or a slanderer they condemned not merely the persons but the very vices that adhered to themselves; it is a well-known saying, he adds, that those who scrutinise others' lives lay claim to every virtue in themselves. Theodoret argues from their own competence: had they received authority to pass sentence they would punish transgressors of the law as guilty, so perfect is their discernment between good and its opposite; it becomes them therefore to see that in the very judgment they pronounce on others they involve themselves in the same condemnation.
2:
We are sure they take as an appeal to what nobody disputes. Barnes calls it the common sentiment of mankind, taught everywhere in the Old Testament; Ellicott says Paul assumes Jew and Gentile will both grant it, with an under-current of allusion to the Jew's habit of falling back on privilege, as though the Gentiles only would be judged and the kingdom his by birth. Wesley hears the same edge: we know it without thy teaching, and the judgment is God's, not thine, who exceptest thyself. Gill fixes what judgment is meant, not what is exercised in this life but what follows after death, called God's in opposition to men's because carried on by him alone, and because it will be definitive. Robertson glosses it only as a decision rendered, good or bad. Clarke reduces it to a sentence: God is impartial, and transgression in a Jew is not less criminal than iniquity in a Gentile. Theodoret says all who transgress the divine law are obnoxious to punishment.

According to truth divides them. Barnes allows the Hebrew sense of certainly but prefers judgment by the real nature of conduct, so the hypocrite no less than the profligate is judged by his true character. Ellicott makes it reality against appearance, status and precedence: the judgment asks what a man is, not to what race he belongs. Calvin calls it a Hebrew idiom for inward integrity, opposed not only to gross falsehood but to the outward appearance of good works, and holds it equivalent to the righteous judgment named later. Wesley says only that it is just and reaches the heart as well as the life.

Whether Paul may reprove before he has proved is Calvin's objection against himself, rhetoricians teaching that reproof should not precede proof. His answer is that the accusation was laid not before men but before conscience, which they could not deny if they examined themselves, and that such men trust themselves with astonishing security unless forcibly shaken; those are besotted who expect to escape God's judgment while allowing none to escape their own. Barnes appeals instead to instinctive conviction and turns it on a standing abuse: crime is crime wherever committed, and Antinomians in all ages, like the Jews, have supposed they may commit with impunity what would be sin in others. He cites Calvin by name for the passage's design. Ellicott and Robertson press the emphatic pronoun, Ellicott asking whether the Jew is the only exception, Robertson making him the conceited Jew expecting to escape because he is a Jew.

The riches of God's goodness Gill and Calvin read as an anticipated objection, not a fresh argument, the difficulty being these men's prosperity. Gill distinguishes the general riches of providential goodness, which the men of the world have the greatest share of, from the special goodness of God's own people; Calvin denies that the verse argues on two grounds, and holds that where the fear of God does not rule, confidence in prosperity mocks his goodness, so a heavier punishment awaits those he has favoured. On the verb he prefers leading as by the hand to driving; Robertson makes the present conative, kindness trying to lead this upstart Jew, who thinks down on God, to a change of mind; Clarke says the end was designed but rendered ineffectual by want of consideration, and quotes the Sohar that God delays his anger so the wicked may repent; Theodoret, that God waits your repentance. Ellicott adds that this use of riches is peculiar to Paul, twelve times in his letters and nowhere else in the New Testament, and protests that the fallacy is not extinct: the bliss of the Christian is reserved for the Christian, not showered promiscuously on all men. Wesley turns the irony of the treasury: the man thinks he is treasuring all good things, and treasures to himself, not to the man he judges.
6:
That judgment goes by works none denies, and the difficulty it raises is Ellicott's subject. He says Paul lays down with unmistakable definiteness that the moral tenor of a life is the standard of its judgment, then asks how this squares with justification by faith. His answer separates two elements in Paul's theology, one common to the Jewish schools and drawn from the Old Testament, the other his own: final recompense by moral action belongs to the first, justification by faith to the second. Mankind is classified at the judgment by the tangible outcome of lives; but the individual before his Judge can claim nothing by works, having broken more commandments than he kept, so his admission must be a divine act conditioned on faith. Calvin reaches a narrower version: God will crown the good works of those he has resolved to glorify, but not on account of merit, and though the verse declares what reward good works have, it does not show what they are worth: it is an absurd inference to deduce merit from reward. Barnes calls it a general principle covering Jew and Gentile, Clarke that he rewards as a man's life has been, Gill that a judgment general to all will be special to each, Theodoret that the obdurate man passes sentence on himself.

Whom the patient continuance describes divides them further. Gill narrows it hard: not the moralised Gentiles, who sought worldly things and popular applause rather than God's honour or the immortality brought to light in the Gospel, nor the pharisaical Jews, who sought righteousness by works of law, but only such as have the true principles of grace implanted. Barnes leaves it open and stresses perseverance rather than a single act. Calvin adds a second virtue: the word means more than perseverance, since patience is required too, by which the saints continue firm under trials, Satan suffering them no free course. Ellicott supplies the verb from the previous verse, treats glory, honour and immortality as equivalent to eternal life, and stresses the patient continuance; Wesley guards the motive, that pure love does not exclude faith, hope and desire; Theodoret says the phrase expresses virtue's difficulties, the verse its crown.

The word rendered contentious is disputed philologically. Ellicott calls the Authorised rendering an error from a wrong derivation: strictly it means those who act in the spirit of a hireling, and thence in a spirit of factiousness and self-seeking. Robertson translates factious outright. Barnes keeps the English word but redirects it: it usually denotes quarrelsomeness among men, but here means a disposition towards God, as good as rebellious. Gill takes it of contending for victory and not truth; Clarke of obstinate dispute against the truth; Wesley makes it personal: like thee, O Jew, who fightest against God. Ellicott adds that the construction changes here from accusative to nominative, and that the two words for anger are the settled feeling and the outbreak.

On the sentence Gill says the terms express the second death, the worm that never dies and the fire not quenched; Clarke, that misery of all descriptions comes without possibility of escape. Ellicott presses that upon every soul of man is not quite upon every man but marks where the punishment will be felt; Robertson takes the word of the individual. Why the Jew comes first they answer alike for different reasons: Calvin because they had, before others, both the promises and the threatenings of the law; Clarke because they abused greater mercies; Wesley because their training in the true religion, and the mission of Christ and his apostles to them first, places them foremost among the criminals; Robertson notes the priority holds in privilege too. Calvin also finds the passage irregular, its tenor interrupted and the clauses of the contrast not cleanly joined; the meaning is not obscure, he says, spiritual wisdom being sought here in a plain style.
10:
On the reward they are brief and agreed. Gill takes glory, honour and peace as so many words for the everlasting happiness of the saints. Wesley sets the three against the three of the previous verse, glory against wrath, honour against indignation, peace against tribulation. Clarke says the man who lives in conscientious obedience to God's known will has them, be he Jew or Gentile.

What no respect of persons excludes they work out at length. Gill lists what will not come into consideration: nation, parentage, age, sex, condition, sect. Calvin says the word covers all outward things commonly thought valuable, kindred, country, dignity, wealth, so that what God regards is purity of heart, and here means the distinction between nations; the verse, he adds, brings the accusation home separately, taking from the Gentiles the subterfuge of ignorance and from the Jews their boasting in the law. Ellicott makes it regard for external circumstances against internal condition, especially birth and race, and says the great result of the Christian revelation was to break down belief in race-religions. Barnes glosses it as partiality in judgment. Robertson adds that Milligan reckons this word and its cognates the earliest known Christian words, absent from the Septuagint. Wesley alone enters a caution: God rewards every one according to his works, yet this is consistent with his distributing opportunities according to his own good pleasure.

Whether the heathen may be saved is the sharpest division, and it turns on what perishing without law implies. Barnes will not soften it: the apostle does not say they shall be saved without law and gives no intimation of their salvation, so that if any heathen are saved it is an exception; the apostles evidently believed the great mass would be destroyed, and on that ground evinced such zeal to save them. Clarke leans the other way: those who transgressed against the mere light of nature, or rather that true light which lighteth every man, do not come under the same rule as the Jews. On the phrase Barnes says it means without written law, since they had a law of nature; Robertson that the adverb ordinarily means contrary to law but here in ignorance of the Mosaic law, and occurs nowhere else in the New Testament; Calvin that the context overrides its common sense; Wesley that it means without regard to any outward law, the man being condemned by the law written in his heart. Ellicott states the principle plainly: each is judged by the method proper to his case, the Jew by the written law and the Gentile by conscience. Gill says the Gentiles lacked Moses but not the law of nature nor civil statutes; Theodoret, that God, being Maker of all, is Judge of all.

The doers of the law shall be justified is the verse Calvin will not let pass. Hearing or knowing the law gives no claim to righteousness; works must be produced, so that if righteousness is sought from the law the law must be fulfilled, its righteousness consisting in perfection of works. Those who pervert the passage to build up justification by works, he says, deserve most fully to be laughed at even by children; the apostle presses only the law's own decision, that transgression draws an instant curse. Wesley reads the two clauses at different times, the hearers not even now just before God, the doers finally acquitted and rewarded. Robertson observes that the law was read in the synagogue but there was no virtue in listening, and compares James; Barnes, that the words meet a Jewish objection; Gill, that hearing without doing never denominates men righteous in God's sight however it recommends them among men; Theodoret, that the law was not sent to gratify our ears but to lead us to right practice. Ellicott alone raises the punctuation: the parenthesis should begin at the next verse, not this one.
14:
By nature is the word they fight over. Clarke will not let it stand for unaided capacity: much stress has been laid on it, he says, as though nature apart from divine grace had principles sufficient to guide a man to glory; he prefers Suicer's sense, truly or in effect, comparing the false gods who certainly are no gods. Ellicott takes it plainly, spontaneously, of their own motion, not under coercion of any external rule; Robertson only parses the case, adding that the Gentiles lack the Mosaic law but not some knowledge of God in conscience, so doing right they are a law to themselves. Gill says Paul owns they had not the written law but intimates they had a law against which they sinned; Barnes extends to the heathen the principle already laid down, that only doers of law are justified by law; Wesley notes that Paul now speaks directly of the heathens to convince them, yet that the concession convinces the Jews more strongly.

What is written in their hearts Calvin defines narrowly, then defends it. The work of the law is what the law requires; they show a discrimination imprinted on their hearts, by which they distinguish just from unjust. He denies that it was engraven on their will so that they pursued it, holding rather that they were so mastered by truth that they could not disapprove it: why else institute religious rites, but that God ought to be worshipped, and why be ashamed of theft, but that they deemed it evil? From this, he insists, the power of the will is deduced without reason, since Paul speaks not of power to fulfil the law but of knowledge of it, and heart here is the understanding, not the seat of the affections. Gill says they had the substance of the law in their minds; Ellicott makes it the practical realisation of the law, written in their hearts as the original was written on tables of stone; Wesley says the same hand wrote both; Robertson that when their conduct corresponds with the Mosaic law they practise the unwritten law in their hearts; Theodoret that conscience judged according to truth.

On conscience they differ in emphasis only. Ellicott finds a double witness, the actions speaking and conscience witnessing with them. Clarke calls it the faculty where the divine light dwells, and reads the doing of justice, mercy and truth as evidence that the law's great object is so far accomplished. Wesley makes it psychological: there is none of all its faculties which the soul has less in its power.

What the last verse attaches to is the clearest disagreement here, and it is one of eras. Calvin's block reports that Jerome, Theophylact and other fathers connected it with the verse before, while almost all modern critics connect it with the twelfth, treating what intervenes as parenthetic. Barnes takes the modern side outright, calling the intervening verses a parenthesis, and Ellicott gives the reason: the verse resumes the main thread and cannot refer to what immediately precedes, since there he describes the daily process by which doubtful actions are submitted to conscience, whereas here he speaks expressly of the final judgment. Wesley alone keeps the older connection, glossing it as who show this in the day. Ellicott adds that as the Son is Mediator of salvation so also of judgment; Cyril presses the same on the conscience: God needs no examination or proofs to condemn, a man is judged out of his own conscience and shall rise clothed with his own sins or his righteous deeds, and it is Christ who judges, the Father judging through the Son. On the last phrase Ellicott asks whether the gospel testifies to the fact of judgment or to its standard, and prefers the fact; Robertson glosses it as what Paul preaches, Clarke as what he now lays down on God's impartiality.
17:
The paragraph's first word is a textual question answered across three centuries. Ellicott calls the Authorised behold a corrupt reading, since a decisive consensus of the best manuscripts has but if; the answering clause is then the question teachest thou not thyself, the therefore there being merely resumptive. Calvin had seen the variant and declined it: were it generally received it would meet his approbation, but the greater part of the manuscripts is opposed and the sense not unsuitable, the whole difference being one letter; the difficulty with the other reading is to find a corresponding clause. His own block carries the sequel, that Griesbach has since found a majority of manuscripts in favour and adopted it. Wesley prints but if, and lays out the structure it implies: twice five articles, the first five what the Jew boasts of in himself, the second five what he glories in over others. Robertson renders bearest the name, surnamed Jew with Lightfoot, and notes that Jew denoted nationality where Hebrew accented language.

Why Paul allows the boast before attacking it they explain alike. Chrysostom says that having shown the Gentile wants nothing for salvation if he be a doer of the law, he sets down the glories of the Jews for which they thought scorn of the Gentiles, beginning with the name itself, of great majesty then as the name Christian is now. Barnes says Paul states their privileges with great skill and address, and adds that though proud, wicked and hypocritical the Jews put the fullest confidence in their religion. Henry says he allows their profession and specifies their pretensions, applying the truth that not the hearers but the doers of the law are justified. Gill says the privileges are granted by an ironical concession, charges following against their principal men. Clarke says that having said enough to convict the conscience, Paul throws off the cover and argues openly, superior knowledge and privilege serving only to aggravate condemnation. Theodoret notes that Paul says not merely named but entitled, and that to rest in the law is not to weary oneself searching after what is right, like a stranger to it, but to have the law itself teaching all things plainly.

What approving the more excellent means is disputed. Barnes says the word bears two senses; Ellicott thinks the Authorised rendering probably right, though the marginal triest the things that differ is possible; Clarke takes the second outright, revelation making the nicest distinctions, and Theodoret likewise, discerning between justice and injustice, temperance and excess, piety and impiety. Calvin cuts across by dividing the act: there is a twofold approval, one of choice, when we embrace the good we approve, and one of judgment only; what he concedes them from the law is the knowledge of God's will and the approval of things useful.

Who the blind and the babes are they dispute. Wesley says flatly that blind, in darkness, ignorant and babes were the titles the Jews generally gave the Gentiles, and Clarke the same; Ellicott points instead to the blind leaders of the blind. Gill turns it inward: all unregenerate men are foolish and need instruction, but here the common people among the Jews, who knew not the law, are meant, it being usual to call their doctors instructors. Barnes distinguishes the two scriptural senses of foolish, the void of understanding and the wicked, and takes the first. Robertson notes that the word for corrector means instructor in Plato, and probably so here, though chastiser in Hebrews, late inscriptions giving it as instructor. On the closing phrase Ellicott says form is not opposed to substance here but implies it, presentation or embodiment; Wesley, the most accurate knowledge of the truth; Calvin makes the clause the ground of their claim to teach, as carrying in their breasts all the secrets of the law; Theodoret says it lays bare their superciliousness towards proselytes.
21:
Whether the clauses are questions or assertions is raised twice. Calvin notes that they are commonly put interrogatively, but that Theophylact, Erasmus and Luther render them as statements, and finds no difference in meaning. Gill says the same, that though put by way of question they are so many assertions and matters of fact. Barnes prefers the question, since the form conveys the truth with greater force and impliedly reproves their ignorance, a teacher of others being expected to be learned himself. Ellicott raises the point again at the boast of the law, where the clause has been read not as a question but as the summary answer to the questions before it; he allows a certain force in that view but rests on the similarity of structure. Robertson describes the syntax instead: Paul breaks off the long sentence begun four verses earlier and starts again with a phrase that gathers it into small compass and drives it home on the Jew. Clarke reproduces Dr. Taylor's paraphrase: what do your pretensions to knowledge and the office of teaching signify, if you have no regard to your own doctrine?

On the charges Gill closes off one escape: adultery here is not to be taken figuratively of adulterating the word of God, but literally, and not in heart only but in act. Barnes says there is no doubt the crime was common, and reports from Grotius that the Talmud accuses celebrated rabbis by name, Josephus giving the same account of the nation. Wesley traces the order: Paul had shown the Gentiles their sins against God, then themselves, then their neighbour, and here charges sin against neighbour, self and God together.

Sacrilege is the charge hardest to place. Ellicott renders it properly rob temples, and takes them to be idol temples, in pointed antithesis to the abhorrence of idols on which the Jew prided himself, adding that it is the last offence we should have expected of Jews of that date, knowing the scrupulousness with which they shunned such things. Robertson keeps the rendering and notes that the verb for abhorring is an old word meaning to make foul, used elsewhere in the New Testament only once. Calvin takes a wider sense: sacrilege is simply a profanation of the divine Majesty, a thing of the same kind as idolatry, and a sin not unknown to the heathen poets, who called men sacrilegious for despising sacred rites.

Where the closing quotation comes from divides them. Calvin thinks it taken from Ezekiel rather than Isaiah, since Isaiah gives no reproofs to the people whereas the chapter in Ezekiel is full of them, though he reports that some take it as an argument from the less to the greater. Ellicott says it is from the Septuagint of Isaiah, whose original sense is that God's name is dishonoured by the enslavement and oppression of his people; Robertson agrees it is a free quotation from that place, and adds the irony that the Jews were so jealous for the Name that they would not pronounce it, yet acted so that the Gentiles blasphemed it. Wesley's block is the bare reference. On the substance Barnes says their hypocrisy and crimes led the pagan world to despise a religion observed to have no better effect on its professors; Clarke quotes a rabbinic saying that rulers destroy the influence of their own words when a teacher in the academy forbids usury and takes it himself; Gill extends the blasphemy to the being and perfections of God and to his law and worship; Calvin adds that though every transgressor dishonours God, a special fault lies here, since they avowed him as their Lawgiver and took no care to form their life by his rule; Theodoret, that through such a man many tongues are excited to speak evil, since those who witness his wicked life reproach the God who chose him.
25:
How far circumcision profits they carefully limit. Wesley does it in four words: the apostle does not say that it justifies. Gill allows the profit only while the rite was in force; Clarke calls it a blessing to wear the covenant's sign, provided its terms are complied with. Calvin says the objection is dissipated by anticipation, circumcision being the symbol of the covenant by which God chose Abraham's seed, so they seemed not to glory in vain. Ellicott glosses the verb sharply, is become, reduced ipso facto to the uncircumcised man's case; Robertson, that the Jew is then like the Gentile, with no privilege at all. Theodoret puts the apostle in the train of the prophecies, where the Gentiles are uncircumcised in flesh and Israel in heart; Henry generalises, that no forms or ordinances can profit without regenerating grace.

Whether the law-keeping Gentile is a real man or a supposition divides them. Gill says the words are spoken hypothetically, if any such could be found among the Gentiles, and hold only of those who from a principle of grace obey the law. Robertson agrees on the grammar, a mere supposition, Paul meaning a keeping kept up perfectly. Clarke takes the case as real: if the Gentile acts according to the spirit and design of the law, and to the light God has afforded, it will be reckoned to him as circumcision. Barnes stands between, ruling out the ceremonial law and referring the words to the moral. Calvin argues from subordination: everything is below its end, so since circumcision looks to the law it is inferior to it, and keeping the law is greater than the rite instituted for its sake. Theodoret answers directly: the law demands practice, so the circumcised who lacks it is justly called a sinner and the uncircumcised who has it takes the name.

On uncircumcision by nature they agree. Gill says that as circumcision was commanded by God and performed by the art of men, uncircumcision is by nature; Barnes calls it man's natural state before admission to any peculiar rite; Clarke, the man whom his country's custom does not oblige. On the judging Ellicott compares the men of Nineveh who shall rise and condemn this generation, the idea being to put to shame by contrast; Barnes makes it condemning as guilty, Robertson notes the unusual distance of the pronoun from its verb. By the letter, he adds, marks the condition under which the action is done, paraphrasable as with all the advantages of law and circumcision; and here again the sentence may be an affirmation, not a question. Calvin warns that the phrase is a figure of speech, not a claim that they violated the law because they had the literal rite.

Who the true Jew is they answer alike. Calvin says a real Jew is not ascertained by descent, profession or external symbol, and that the circumcision which constitutes a Jew is not an outward sign only, both being inward; he calls the outward rite without piety the letter and its spiritual design the spirit, since the importance of signs depends on their design, and when that is disregarded the letter alone remains. Gill distinguishes between a Jew and a Jew and between circumcision and circumcision: the inward man has not an outward name only but an inward nature, the law not in hand but in heart. Barnes says he comes up to the design of the Jewish institution. Clarke calls him a true member of the Church of God, his heart purified as the prophets prescribe; Wesley refers the acceptable circumcision to the promise in Deuteronomy, the putting away of all inward impurity; Henry presses the parallel home, that a man is no more a Christian now than he was really a Jew of old who is only one outwardly, nor is that baptism which is outward in the flesh.
